sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: [p. 21] Engineering properties of soils are those properties which can be used for evaluating the ultimate and serviceability limit states (such as shear strength, compressibility, permeability). This chapter considers engineering properties of soil that are useful in designing shallow foundations using static methods. Limited discussions on dynamic soil properties are included in this chapter; more details of dynamic properties are discussed in Chapter 9.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-1, printed p. 21.

sections.title: Influence depths
sections.body: [p. 21] Influence depths. Supporting soils can be influenced to certain depths depending on foundation type, size, load application, and other soil-structure interactions. These depths are identified as influence zones and can vary based on the limit state evaluated. Soil properties should be evaluated within the load influence zones. In addition, the geotechnical engineer should also be familiar with major geologic processes that have and can affect the project site so that soil and rock conditions outside of the influence zones do not negatively impact foundation performance.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-1a, printed p. 21.

sections.title: Methods of determining soil properties
sections.body: [p. 21] Methods of determining soil properties. Engineering soil properties of geologic strata or imported fill are typically estimated using (1) in situ test data from field explorations, (2) laboratory testing, and (3) empirical correlations. In situ and laboratory tests should be performed using ASTM procedures.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-1b, printed p. 21.

sections.title: Purpose of guidance tables and charts
sections.body: [p. 21] Purpose of guidance tables and charts. Tables and charts based on index properties (such as grain size, Atterberg limits, and water contents) are useful for initial estimates or checking the reasonableness of design parameters. However, these correlations can incorporate a higher level of uncertainties and should be used with caution. The final design parameters should be based on in situ test results (such as standard penetration test [SPT], cone penetration test [CPT], Becker Penetration Test [BPT], and vane shear tests [VST]), laboratory test results on relatively undisturbed or disturbed soils based on soil types, or appropriate empirical relationships. Use of empirical correlations should be based on in situ or laboratory test data and should be evaluated based on successful applications in local geologic conditions (whichever is more reliable).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-1c, printed p. 21.

sections.title: Reference guidelines
sections.body: [p. 21] Reference guidelines. Several national agencies including USACE have developed guidelines for soil parameters that should be reviewed by the practitioners for background, development, and application of soil parameters.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-1d, printed p. 21.

sections.title: Main categories of soil parameters analyses and design
sections.body: [p. 21] Soil parameters for static analyses of shallow foundations fall into four main categories: (1) water flow characteristics, hydraulic conductivity, and coefficient of consolidation, (2) strength, (3) volume change (compressibility), and (4) shear distortion (stiffness).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2, printed p. 21.

sections.title: Water flow characteristics
sections.body: [p. 22] Water flow characteristics. The rate at which water moves through the soil as a function of a hydraulic gradient or a change in volume. These are generally characterized using vertical and horizontal hydraulic conductivity (kv and kh, respectively) and coefficient of consolidation (vertical Cv and horizontal Ch). Coefficient of consolidation (Cv) provides estimates of rate of consolidation due to loading and is generally measured from deformation versus time data from laboratory consolidation testing.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2a, printed p. 22.

sections.title: Shear strength
sections.body: [p. 22] Shear strength. Soil shear strength is defined as the ultimate resistance to shear stresses imposed by structures in static or dynamic conditions. A key consideration for evaluation shear strength is whether the soil will be drained or undrained during loading.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2b, printed p. 22.

sections.title: Drained conditions (effective stress parameters)
sections.body: [p. 22] Drained conditions (effective stress parameters). For coarse-grained soils with relatively high permeability, or where the rate of loading is relatively slow, drained conditions should be evaluated. Pore pressures near equilibrium can be estimated from the position of the water table, or by flownet solution if flow is present. Effective stress parameters are used for evaluation of drained conditions. For moderately consolidated to overconsolidated clays and plastic silts, both drained and undrained strength parameters should be evaluated, and design should reflect both end of construction and long-term conditions. For coarse-grained soils (such as sand, gravel), drained strength is often more critical. Drained conditions are also critical for settlement analyses.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2b(1), printed p. 22.

sections.title: Undrained conditions (total stress parameters)
sections.body: [p. 22] Undrained conditions (total stress parameters). For fine-grained soil with relatively low permeability, or if the rate of loading is relatively fast, undrained conditions should be evaluated. For undrained conditions, pore pressures will be unknown and only total stresses can be estimated. Therefore, total stress parameters are used for evaluation of undrained conditions. For normally consolidated to slightly overconsolidated clays and plastic silt with overconsolidation ratio, OCR < 4, undrained soil strengths could be more critical. Overconsolidation ratio (OCR) is defined as the ratio of the preconsolidation stress (σ′p) to the existing vertical effective overburden stress (σ′vo).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2b(2), printed p. 22.

sections.title: Peak strength condition
sections.body: [p. 22] Peak strength condition. Soil strength for peak strength condition is generally characterized by using shear stress at failure (τf) through the undrained strength (τf = su), drained friction angle (τf = σ′n tan φ′), or combination of effective stress cohesion and drained friction angle for peak strength (τf = c′ + σ′n tan φ′). Drained soil parameters are also identified as effective strength parameters and thus, “drained strength parameter” and “effective strength parameter” are used interchangeably.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2b(3), printed p. 22.

sections.title: Design strength
sections.body: [p. 22] Design strength. In general, shallow foundations are designed for peak soil strengths using drained soil parameters (c′ and φ′) or undrained strength (su). However, for seismic analysis, or evaluating performance of an existing foundation, other soil strengths associated with higher strains such as such as critical state strength, fully softened strength, and residual strength may be needed. EM 1110-2-1902 should be used for guidance for these strength parameters. For dynamic analyses of shallow foundations, guidance is provided in Chapter 9.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2b(4), printed p. 22.

sections.title: Volume change (compression)
sections.body: [p. 23] Volume change (compression).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2c, printed p. 23.

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 23] General. Volume changes can occur due to changes in effective stresses. This can be visualized as the change in size of a soil element. The effective stress level with shallow foundation loading relative to the maximum effective stress level the soil has experienced is important to estimate the volume change due to foundation loading. Chapter 7 provides detail procedures to estimate settlement using laboratory testing. This chapter provides typical values of compression indexes.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2c(1), printed p. 23.

sections.title: Consolidation test parameters
sections.body: [p. 23] Consolidation test parameters. Volume change in soil due to shallow foundation loadings in fine-grained soils are generally characterized by consolidation-related parameters (such as compression index, Cc, recompression index, Cr, and coefficient of secondary settlement, Cα). These parameters are generally estimated from consolidation testing. Definition of these parameters are as follows,

sections.body: [p. 23] Compression index (Cc), is the slope of the virgin compression part of the void ratio (e) versus effective vertical stress (σ′z) curve from the consolidation test.

sections.body: [p. 23] Secondary compression index (Cα), is the ratio of the change in void ratio (Δe) and logarithm of time curve between time of interest (t), expressed as [Δlog(t) = log(t1) − log(t2)] from a part of the void ratio versus logarithm of time curve.

sections.title: Stiffness
sections.body: [p. 23] Stiffness. Stiffness properties of soil are relationships that relate stress to strain. The four main stiffness relationships used in foundation analysis and design are the shear modulus (G), elastic modulus (E), constrained modulus (M) and bulk modulus (K). These different stiffness relationships are related, and if one is known, the others can be determined using Poison’s ratio. Stiffness parameters and typical values are discussed in paragraph 3-9. Figure 3-13 illustrates the different stiffness definitions. The stiffness parameters can be determined by laboratory testing, in situ testing, and correlation with other properties.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2d, printed p. 23.

sections.title: Shear modulus
sections.body: [p. 23] Shear modulus. The shear modulus (G) is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain. This is described as shear distortion and can be visualized as the change in shape of a soil element. The shear modulus is used primarily in numerical modeling of excavations, large embankments, retaining structures, and other situations where soil shear stresses and shear distortion are of concern.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2d(1), printed p. 23.

sections.title: Elastic modulus
sections.body: [p. 23] Elastic modulus. The elastic modulus, E (also Young’s modulus), is the ratio of normal stress to normal strain in the same direction. E is used in many foundation analysis settlement solutions in which the ground is treated as an infinite elastic half-space. Soil behavior generally has a non-linear, stress-strain relationship, and therefore, care should be taken to apply E for the stress range under consideration.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2d(2), printed p. 23.

sections.title: Constrained modulus
sections.body: [p. 24] Constrained modulus. The constrained modulus (M) is the ratio of normal stress to strain in the loading direction when the ground is constrained from movement in the perpendicular directions. Some settlement analysis formulas use M to estimate vertical displacements under foundation loads, under the assumption that there is no horizontal ground strain.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2d(3), printed p. 24.

sections.title: Bulk modulus
sections.body: [p. 24] Bulk modulus. Bulk modulus (K) is the ratio of the mean stress to the volumetric strain. The bulk modulus is used primarily in certain numerical constitutive model formulations methods for estimating ground deformation patterns, however, most routine shallow foundation problems do not use the bulk modulus in settlement estimates.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-2d(4), printed p. 24.

Organic soils have a lower specific gravity, and soils with heavy metallic minerals have a higher specific gravity. In practice, in situ unit weight is generally calculated from in situ water content (w) and dry unit weight (γd).

sections.title: Relative density
sections.body: [p. 27] Relative density (DR) represents the relative denseness or looseness of a soil layer and applies to soils having less than 15 percent fines. Laboratory and in situ tests can be performed to estimate relative density of soils. Different in situ soil index parameters (such as normalized SPT blow counts (N1)60cs, CPT tip resistance, CPT-qc) can provide quantitative measures for relative denseness of coarse-grained soils.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-4, printed p. 27.

sections.title: Relative density and void ratio of coarse-grained soils
sections.body:
[p. 28] Relative density and void ratio of coarse-grained soils. Relative density of coarse-grained soils compares the void ratio of a given soil with the maximum void ratio (emax) and minimum void ratio (emin). The void ratio (e) is defined by equation 3-1. Typical values of void ratios for sand vary from about 0.4 to 1.0, and typical values of clays vary from about 0.3 to 1.5. Higher void ratios can be present for some organic soils (Holtz et al. 2011).

e = Vv/Vs [Eq. 3-1]

where:
e = void ratio (expressed as a decimal)
Vv = volume of voids (ft^3)
Vs = volume of solids (ft^3)

sections.title: The maximum and minimum dry density of a soil can be obtained from laboratory …
sections.body: [p. 29] The maximum and minimum dry density of a soil can be obtained from laboratory testing. The maximum dry density is obtained from laboratory testing ASTM D4253, Standard Test Methods for Maximum Index Density and Unit Weight of Soils Using a Vibratory Table. The minimum dry density is obtained from laboratory testing ASTM D4254, Standard Test Methods for Minimum Index Density and Unit Weight of Soils and Calculation of Relative Density.

sections.title: These test methods (ASTM D4253 and ASTM D4254) are applicable to soils that …
sections.body: [p. 29] These test methods (ASTM D4253 and ASTM D4254) are applicable to soils that contain up to 15 percent, by dry mass, of soil particles passing a No. 200 sieve, provided they still have cohesionless, free-draining characteristics. Further, these test methods are applicable to soils in which 100 percent, by dry mass, of soil particles pass a 3-inch sieve. In case of soils that contain larger particles, scalping of particles larger than 3 inches is performed for this testing.

sections.title: In situ test methods
sections.body: [p. 29] In situ test methods. The in situ void ratio (e) or dry density (γd) of soil can be obtained from a sand cone test (ASTM D1556) or a large-diameter ring density test (ASTM D4914 or ASTM D5030). Sand cone tests (ASTM D1556) are not suitable for soils consisting of unbound granular materials that will not maintain stable sides in the test hole, soils containing appreciable amounts of coarse materials larger than 1.5 inches, and granular soils having high void ratios (very loose soils). When materials contain appreciable amounts of particles larger than 1.5 inch, or when test hole volumes larger than 0.1 ft^3 are required, test method ASTM D4914 or ASTM D5030 are used.

sections.title: Terzaghi and Peck (1948) first developed a relationship between relative …
sections.body:
[p. 29] Terzaghi and Peck (1948) first developed a relationship between relative density (DR) and SPT N-values. Meyerhof (1957) developed a relationship between SPT N-values and relative density of clean sands based on chamber tests. Skempton (1986) used laboratory and field test data from the United States and Japan to provide guidance on the relationship between SPT N-values and relative density. SPT N-values corrected for overburden pressure (N1)60 and relative density (DR) are related based on equation 3-4.

[p. 30] DR = √((N1)60/Cd) × 100(%) [Eq. 3-4]

where:
DR = relative density (%)
(N1)60 = normalized SPT N-Value, (N1)60 = N60 · CN Skempton (1986) suggested that for fine sands (N1)60 values should be reduced in the ratio of 55/60 and for coarse sands, (N1)60 values should be increased in the ratio of 65/60.

Nm = measured SPT N-value in field per ASTM D1586 (blows/ft)
CN = overburden stress correction factor, equation 4-6

sections.title: Skempton (1986) found that the relative density of sand depends on overburden …
sections.body: [p. 30] Skempton (1986) found that the relative density of sand depends on overburden pressure, SPT N60 value, particle, size, soil aging, and overconsolidation. Selection of appropriate Cd is an important part of relative density estimation from in situ index properties such as (N1)60. Skempton found good conformance with Terzaghi and Peck’s (1948) classification using Cd ≈ 60.

sections.title: Cubrinovski and Ishihara (1999) compiled results of 61 relative density …
sections.body: [p. 30] Cubrinovski and Ishihara (1999) compiled results of 61 relative density measurements performed on sands and gravel samples, where SPT data of known (N1)78 blow counts (Japanese energy ratio of 78 percent) were available. The relationship of emax – emin for sand and gravel (equation 3-5), suggested by Cubrinovski and Ishihara (1999), is based on D50 values (particle diameter at 50 percent in the cumulative distribution). However, as discussed in paragraph 3-4c, emax – emin values can be more accurately developed using laboratory tests ASTM D4253 and ASTM D4254. Figure 3-1 shows a relationship between emax – emin and D50 of sand and gravel.

sections.title: Equation 3-6 can be used for Cd estimation for relating to SPT (N1)60 values
sections.body:
[p. 30] Equation 3-6 can be used for Cd estimation for relating to SPT (N1)60 values. Equation 3-6 has been converted from original Cubrinovski and Ishihara (1999) relationship for use in U.S. practice of SPT (N1)60. In general, Cd values of 45 reflect silty sand, 60 reflects clean sands to gravelly sand, and 60 to 70 reflects gravelly soil to gravel.

emax − emin = 0.23 + 0.06/D50 [Eq. 3-5]

[p. 31] where:
emax = void ratio of cohesionless soil in its loosest state
emin = void ratio of cohesionless in its densest state
D50 = particle size corresponding to 50 percent finer on the cumulative particle size distribution curve (mm)

Cd = 11.7/(emax − emin)^1.7   for hammer energy ratio = 60% [Eq. 3-6]

where:
Cd = parameter representing the grain-size effects, and therefore, function of emax – emin
emax = void ratio of cohesionless soil in its loosest state
emin = void ratio of cohesionless in its densest state

sections.title: In soils with gravel, the soil behavior will depend on quantity, distribution …
sections.body: [p. 32] In soils with gravel, the soil behavior will depend on quantity, distribution, and size of gravel particles (percent retained on #4 sieve) as well as the characteristics of the other soil particles. Gravels could be in particle-to-particle contact in soils with higher gravel contents or stay in a soil matrix without particle contacts. If gravel particles stay in a soil matrix, the soil behaviors could be predominantly influenced by the other soil types in the matrix, such as sand, silt, and clay. In this case, gravel particles could float in a soil matrix. However, if gravel particles are in particle-to-particle contact, the probability of particle breakage could increase due to stress concentration at smaller contact areas.

sections.title: In both cases, SPT or CPT measurements tend higher than for a sand at a similar …
sections.body: [p. 32] In both cases, SPT or CPT measurements tend higher than for a sand at a similar relative density. Gravel or larger particle contents as low as 5 to 10 percent can result in higher SPT N60 or CPT-tip resistance, whereas the soil behavior tends be influenced by other soil types in the matrix.

sections.title: Relative density for gravel can be used to estimate the in situ state of …
sections.body:
[p. 32] Relative density for gravel can be used to estimate the in situ state of gravelly materials. Rollins (1998) used Cd = 70 to estimate relative density (DR) and shear modulus of gravelly soils, when using equation 3-4. Cubrinovski and Ishihara (1999) can be used for gravelly soils, as the database includes both sand and gravel soils (equation 3-5 and 3-6). Menq (2003) compiled (emax – emin) data from different studies in the United States and Japan (Figure 3-2) to develop a relationship for emax – emin, emax, and emin, based on Cu.

Note. It is not apparent from Menq (2003) whether the tests in the database were performed with scalping particles larger than 3 inches, as required in ASTM D4253 and ASTM D4254. A gradation of 3 inches minus should be used in equations 3-7 to 3-9 to appropriately capture the portion of the soil matrix that would most influence behaviors.

emax − emin = 0.35 (1/Cu) + 0.21, if 200 ≥ Cu ≥ 2 [Eq. 3-7]

emax = 0.95 (1/Cu) + 0.43, if 200 ≥ Cu ≥ 1 [Eq. 3-8]

emin = 0.60 (1/Cu) + 0.22, if 200 ≥ Cu ≥ 2 [Eq. 3-9]

where:
emax = void ratio of cohesionless soil in its loosest state
emin = void ratio of cohesionless in its densest state
Cu = uniformity coefficient of soil from gradation tests (D60 / D10)
D60 = particle size corresponding to 60% finer on the cumulative particle size distribution curve (mm)
D10 = particle size corresponding to 10% finer on the cumulative particle size distribution curve (mm)

[p. 33] Figure 3-2. Variation of (emax – emin) with uniformity coefficient, Cu of gravelly materials tested in the United States and Japan (Winterkom and Fang 1975; Kokusho et al. 1995; Rix 1984) (Figure adopted from Menq 2003)

Note: As shown in Figure 3-2, scatter in data is significant. For example, for a uniformity coefficient, Cu = 50, emax – emin results from the database vary between 0.2 and 0.32. To reduce unconservative bias in using this dataset, the gradation curves (after adjusting by removing materials greater than 3-inch particles) should be used to calculate Cu. It will be consistent with protocol for ASTM D4253 and ASTM D4254. The adjustment should provide a more realistic basis for the engineering properties for the soil portions that would control design and performance of a shallow foundation.

sections.title: Drained shear strength parameters
sections.body: [p. 33] Drained shear strength parameters are generally cohesion intercept (c′) and drained friction angle (φ′). In situ and laboratory tests can be used for φ′ estimation. Laboratory tests can be used to estimate cohesion intercept (c′). However, it is typical to neglect c′ in shallow foundation design considering that the values are usually low. This section provides typical values and correlations for estimating drained friction angle.

sections.body: [p. 33] Evaluation of strength states or similar calculations for shallow foundation design require strength parameters at shallower depths up to the influence zones, with considerations for outside the influence zones. sections.body:
[p. 33] With construction of the shallow foundation and structures, overburden stress increases. Stress-normalized strength relationships (based on overburden stress-corrected blow counts or tip resistance) have potential to overestimate drained friction angle of coarse-grained soils at shallower depths. Considering the limitations regarding [p. 34] in situ testing and empirical relationships for shallow depths, Table 3-6 can be used to estimate drained friction angle of coarse-grained soils at shallow depths. The table is based on different geotechnical design textbooks and manuals.

sections.title: Drained friction angle of sand from standard penetration test
sections.body:
[p. 34] Drained friction angle of sand from standard penetration test. The friction angle of sand can be expressed for different states such as peak friction angle (φ′peak), critical state friction angle (φ′cv), and residual state friction angle (φ′rs). As shallow foundations are not designed for post-peak strength or large-strain conditions, peak friction angle is applicable for shallow foundation design. An SPT N-value-based relationship by Hatanaka and Uchida (1996) is widely used for estimating the drained friction angle of sand (Figure 3-3). The Hatanaka and Uchida (1996) database includes clean sand (~1 percent fines) to silty sand (up to 30 percent fines).

φ′ = 20° + √(15.4 (N1)60)   (Hatanaka and Uchida 1996) [Eq. 3-10]

where:
φ′ = drained friction angle (degrees), see note
(N1)60 = normalized SPT N-Value (bpf), (N1)60 = N60 · CN
N60 = SPT N-value corrected to 60 percent of the theoretical free-fall hammer energy (bpf), reference equation 4-4
CN = overburden stress correction factor; equation 4-6

Note. This relationship has potential to overestimate drained friction angle for design at shallow depths. A comparison with Table 3-6 should be performed to estimate drained friction angle. Values greater than 36 degrees should be generally avoided for shallow foundation design.

sections.body:
[p. 35] Drained friction angle of sand from CPTu. The drained friction angle (φ′) of sand can be estimated from equation 3-11 (Uzielli et al. 2013) as illustrated in Figure 3-4. This equation is applicable for clean quartz to silica sands where the CPTu soundings are advanced at a rate of 0.787 inches/sec or less, pore water pressures are essentially hydrostatic (pore water ratio, Bq = 0, reference Table 4-7), and the soil behavior type index, Ic < 2.6.

φ′ = 25° (qt1)^0.10   (Uzielli et al. 2013) [Eq. 3-11]

where:
φ′ = drained friction angle (degrees), see note
qt1 = stress-normalized CPT resistance for sands, (qt/Patm)/(σ′vo/Patm)^0.5 same units as Patm
qt = corrected total cone resistance (same unit as Patm)
Patm = atmospheric pressure (at sea level Pa ≈ 2,116.2 psf or 101.3 kPa)
σ′vo = in situ vertical effective stress (same unit as Patm)

Note. This relationship has potential to overestimate drained friction angle for design of shallow foundations at shallow depths. A comparison with Table 3-6 should be performed to estimate drained friction angle. Values greater than 36 degrees should generally be avoided for shallow foundation design.

sections.title: Drained friction angle of sand from dilatometer
sections.body:
[p. 36] Drained friction angle of sand from dilatometer. A series of direct relationships between the effective stress friction angle of clean sands (φ′) at peak strength to the dilatometer text (DMT) horizontal stress index (KD) were developed by Marchetti (1997) as illustrated in Figure 3-5. The relationships were developed for several specific horizontal stress conditions. A lower bound solution from (Marchetti 1997) is shown in equation 3-12. For clean sands, equation 3-13 (Rix et al. 2018) can also be used.

φ′ = 28.0° + 14.6 · log(KD) − 2.1 · log[(KD)]^2   (Marchetti 1997) [Eq. 3-12]

φ′ = 20.0° + [0.04 + 0.06 · (KD)^(−1)]^(−1)   (Rix et al.2018) [Eq. 3-13]

where:
φ′ = drained friction angle (degrees), see note
KD = horizontal stress index, see equation 4-14

Note. Equation 3-12 tends to underpredict the drained friction angle by approximately 2° to 4°. A comparison with Table 3-6 should be performed to estimate drained friction angle. Values greater than 36 degrees should be generally avoided for shallow foundation design.

sections.title: Undrained shear strength
sections.body: [p. 39] Undrained shear strength (su) values vary in response to a particular loading condition, and is, therefore, stress path-dependent. Generally, su varies over depth as a function of in situ confining stress.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-6, printed p. 39.

sections.title: Undrained shear strength of clay from standard penetration test
sections.body: [p. 39] Undrained shear strength of clay from standard penetration test. For soft to firm intact clays and structured or sensitive clays, the dynamic energy of the SPT is inappropriate and correlations with undrained shear strength could be unreliable. In the case of stiff to hard, insensitive clays, the SPT may be used to estimate undrained shear strength. Even for these clays, site-specific relationships for a given clay in a [p. 40] particular geologic setting should be developed, considering geologic setting, plasticity, origin, and other aspects of the clay formation (Rix et al. 2018).

sections.title: Undrained shear strength of clay from cone penetration test
sections.body:
[p. 40] Undrained shear strength of clay from cone penetration test. CPTs are commonly used for undrained shear strength (su) estimates using equation 3-14. The su estimates based on cone penetration data depend on the empirical cone factor.

su = (qt − σvo)/Nkt [Eq. 3-14]

where:
su = undrained shear strength (tsf)
qt = total cone resistance (tsf)
σvo = total in situ vertical stress (tsf)
Nkt = empirical cone factors, see Note

Note. Empirical cone factor (Nkt) values have been found to range between 6 and 30, with commonly used values ranging from 12 to 15 (Lunne et al. 1997). Robertson and Cabal (2022) recommends an average value of 14. Multiple studies suggest that Nkt increases with increasing plasticity and decreases with increasing soil sensitivity. For very sensitive, fine-grained soils, values as low as 6 are reported. In many projects, an Nkt value of 15 is assumed without consideration of the actual site-specific soil conditions or predominant shear modes. In critical projects, laboratory tests from adjacent borings should be performed to determine site-specific Nkt values.

σ′vc = initial vertical effective stress, prior to blade penetration (tsf)
KD = horizontal stress index, see equation 4-14

sections.title: Undrained shear strength using SHANSEP (stress history and normalized soil engineering properties) method
sections.body: [p. 41] Undrained shear strength using SHANSEP (stress history and normalized soil engineering properties) method. Soil strength of plastic, fine-grained soils due to shallow foundation loading depends on stress history of soils. The overconsolidation ratio (OCR), established from an oedometer test, is a common measure of stress history of soil, reference paragraph 6-5d. A plastic, fine-grained soil that has experienced higher loading in the past due to geologic processes (such as glaciation) or artificial preloading or groundwater level change, or drainage, etc., has a higher OCR than a soil that has not been subjected to subsequent loading. If a soil is loaded and then unloaded, it retains part of its stress history, which can then influence soil behavior if it is later reloaded (Holtz et al. 2011).

sections.body:
[p. 41] General. The undrained shear strength ratio in clayey soils increases with increasing OCR. Ladd and Foote (1974) developed the SHANSEP method to estimate undrained strengths of clayey soils. This procedure also reduces impacts of disturbances that could occur in soil sample collection, transportation, sample preparation, and laboratory testing. Equation 3-16 relates undrained strength ratio with OCR. Figure 3-9 presents examples of su/σ′vc vs. OCR for different soils (Ladd et al. 1977).

OCR = overconsolidation ratio

sections.title: Undrained shear strength from vane shear strength tests
sections.body: [p. 44] Undrained shear strength from vane shear strength tests. Vane shear testing is a useful method for determining undrained shear strength (su), stress history, and sensitivity in soft clays, silts, and organic soils. VSTs are not applicable in sandy soils or non-plastic silts as these can allow drainage during testing. VSTs should be performed according to ASTM D2573. Field vane shear strength values require correction based on plasticity index (PI) values to calculate mobilized shear strength. Bjerrum’s (1973) correction factor (μ) has been commonly used to calculate mobilized shear strength (equation 3-18 and Figure 3-11). ASTM D2573 also presents the vane shear correction factor (μR), as per Chandler (1988) and Aas et al. (1988) for determining su. The Chandler correction factor depends on time to failure, along with PI.

sections.title: Determination of overconsolidation ratio from vane shear test results
sections.body: [p. 44] Determination of overconsolidation ratio from vane shear test results. The undrained shear strength of softer soils, as measured by the VSTs can be used to estimate OCR using the SHANSEP relationship (Ladd and Foote 1974; Ladd et al. 1977; and Ladd 1991).

sections.title: Sensitivity of soft soils
sections.body:
[p. 44] Sensitivity of soft soils. Sensitivity of soft soils can be calculated as the ratio of peak to remolded shear strengths. Sensitivity of soft soils is a useful index to estimate residual strength at large deformations. It can be important for slope stability of shallow structures on slopes or conditions where construction of a structure on shallow foundation on soft soils may induce large deformations. Slope stability is not covered in this manual.

(su)fv = peak undrained shear strength from field vane shear test (tsf)

sections.title: Consolidation and rate of consolidation parameters
sections.body: [p. 45] Consolidation theory is described in geotechnical engineering textbooks. Section 7-9 provides step-by-step procedures for estimating consolidation parameters from laboratory consolidation test data. This section provides typical values and empirical relationships for consolidation and rate of consolidation parameters that can be used to evaluate the reasonableness of laboratory test results.

sections.title: Compression and recompression ratios
sections.body:
[p. 47] Compression and recompression ratios. Values of compression index (Cc) and recompression index (Cr) can be normalized with respect to the void space available in the soil by dividing by (1+e0) as shown in equations 3-19 and 3-20. The resulting values are expressed in terms of vertical strain (such as Cεc and Cεr) and can be used as an alternative to estimating the compression and recompression indices directly where the initial void ratio is known. For soils of similar geologic origin, site-specific correlations can be established for Cεc and Cεr versus initial void ratio. Ranges of compression ratio (Cεc) and recompression ratio (Cεr) for different classifications of soil compressibility are provided in Table 3-10 (Coduto et al. 2016).

Compression Ratio, Cεc = Cc/(1 + e0) [Eq. 3-19]

Recompression Ratio, Cεr = Cr/(1 + e0) [Eq. 3-20]

sections.title: Coefficient of consolidation
sections.body: [p. 47] Coefficient of consolidation. The coefficient of consolidation (Cv) is a key parameter used to describe the rate at which saturated clay or other soil undergoes consolidation when subjected to an increase in effective stress. Larger Cv values indicate faster consolidation. In general, Cv is greater for stiff clays than soft clays. [p. 48] Often, consolidation is faster in the field than determined in a laboratory due to sand seams and fissures that can shorten the drainage path.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-7c, printed pp. 47 to 48.

sections.title: Laboratory determination of Cv and correlations with liquid limit
sections.body:
[p. 48] Laboratory determination of Cv and correlations with liquid limit. For incremental stress consolidation tests (ASTM D2435), Cv can be calculated from the time curves using one of several different methods, reference paragraph 7-18c. For the constant rate of strain (CRS) consolidation test (ASTM D4186), Cv can be calculated at every point where the excess pore water pressure, average stress, and strain are known. The CRS consolidation test provides increased resolution of the compression curve in the vicinity of the preconsolidation stress. CRS testing also allows the determination of the coefficient of consolidation (Cv) over the entire range of loading as long as the excess pore water pressures are in an acceptable range. Table 3-11 presents typical values of coefficient of consolidation (Cv). Correlations between coefficient of consolidation and liquid limit are shown in Figure 3-12.

sections.body:
[p. 49] Hydraulic conductivity relationship with coefficient of consolidation. Hydraulic conductivity (k) can be indirectly calculated at each loading step based on Terzaghi’s consolidation theory per equation 3-21. Indirect methods tend to give much lower hydraulic conductivity values in the low-compressibility zone. Mesri et al. (1994) reported that the indirect method typically underestimates the value of permeability by a factor of 2.

Hydraulic Conductivity, k = Cv · mv · γw [Eq. 3-21]

where:
k = hydraulic conductivity or permeability (ft/sec)
Cv = coefficient of consolidation (ft^2/sec), reference paragraph 7-18c
mv = coefficient of volumetric consolidation (psf^(-1))
γw = unit weight of water (pcf)

sections.title: Coefficient of secondary compression
sections.body: [p. 49] Coefficient of secondary compression.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-7d, printed p. 49.

sections.title: General
sections.body:
[p. 49] General. The coefficient of secondary compression (Cα) is defined as the creep deformation over one log cycle of time, t following the end of primary consolidation. The magnitude of Cα is stress-dependent for a particular soil and should be determined at an effective stress similar to that expected in situ. Soil compressibility is characterized for Cα in Table 3-12. As with the compression ratios, the coefficient of secondary compression can be defined as function of strain (Cεα) or as a function of the void ratio Cα. Mesri (1973) summarized the data shown in Figure 3-13 to estimate the modified secondary compression index (Cεα) of NC clays using the natural water [p. 50] content. Based on that data, Cεα can be estimated using equation 3-22. For overconsolidated clays, Cεα generally ranges from 0.0005 and 0.001 (Kulhawy and Mayne 1990). The procedure for estimating the coefficient of secondary compression from oedometer test data is addressed in paragraph 7-19.

Cεα = Cα/(1 + e) = 0.0001 ωn [Eq. 3-22]

Cεα = modified secondary compression index
Cα = coefficient of secondary compression
ωn = natural water content (%)

sections.title: Preconsolidation stress and overconsolidation ratio from standard penetration test
sections.body:
[p. 51] Preconsolidation stress and overconsolidation ratio from standard penetration test. Empirical correlations can be used to estimate the OCR of a sand. For OCR in sands, silty sands, and sandy silts, equation 3-23 (Mayne 2007a) can be used. Equation 3-24, suggested by Kulhawy and Chen 2007, is intended for gravels. For sandy soils, preconsolidation stress can be more difficult to estimate due to difficulties in separating the effects of relative density from OCR.

OCR = σ′p/σ′zo = (0.468 Pa · (N60)^m)/σ′zo   (sands, silty sand, sandy silts) [Eq. 3-23]

σ′zo = initial vertical effective stress (tsf)
Pa = atmospheric pressure (tsf), 1 Pa ≈ 1 tsf

m = exponent, 0.6 for clean quartzite sands or 0.8 for silty sands to sandy silts (such as Piedmont), 1.0 for intact clays and clayey silts

sections.title: Preconsolidation stress from cone penetration test

[p. 52] Preconsolidation stress from cone penetration test. Mayne 2014 suggested a correlation expressed as equation 3-25, which applies to clays and sands. The correlation was derived from cavity expansion—critical state solution for clays, large calibration chamber tests on sand, and field and laboratory data worldwide. The interpreted σ′p results should be compared with other information, such as oedometer results on high-quality, undisturbed samples, as well as geologic stress history. Additional corroboration may be obtained by comparison with other in situ tests, such as DMT and/or VST.

sections.title: Overconsolidation ratio from dilatometer
sections.body:
[p. 53] Overconsolidation ratio from dilatometer. OCR can be calculated for uncemented clays with ID < 1.2 and sands/silts with ID > 1.2 using equation 3-26 (Marchetti 1980). Kulhawy and Mayne (1990) showed test data suggesting that the coefficient 0.5 in equation 3-26 can vary in the range of 0.27 to 0.75 depending on the degree of fissuring, sensitivity, and geologic origin. For all soil types, equation 3-27 (Marchetti 1980) can be used.

OCR = (0.5KD)^1.56 [Eq. 3-26]

where:
OCR = overconsolidation ratio (dimensionless)
KD = horizontal stress index, see equation 4-14

Note. For NC clays with OCR = 1, KD = 2. This correlation does not apply to “cemented-structured-aged” clays. It is more difficult to correlate DMT data with OCR of sands, and only very rough estimates can be obtained using both M from DMT data and qc from the CPT.

OCR ≈ 0.51(po − uo) [Eq. 3-27]

where:
OCR = overconsolidation ratio (dimensionless)
po = contact stress or corrected A-Reading (kPa), reference equation 4-10
uo = hydrostatic pore water pressure (kPa), reference equation 4-12

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 53] General. The hydraulic conductivity (k) depends primarily on the size and shape of the soil grains, void ratio, shape and arrangement of voids, degree of saturation, and temperature. Hydraulic conductivity of soil in saturated conditions is typically used for steady-state seepage analyses. Time-dependent settlement of soil depends on its [p. 54] hydraulic conductivity, among other factors. Hydraulic conductivity parameters are required to evaluate drainage conditions, uplift pressure, and time rate of settlement. EM 1110-2-1901 and EM 1110-2-1913 provide guidance for determining hydraulic conductivity of different types of soils. Hydraulic conductivity of fine-grained soils should be obtained from laboratory tests or guidance provided in EM 1110-2-1901 and EM 1110-2-1913.

sections.title: Empirical equations such as Kozeny-Carman and Hazen equations have been …
sections.body: [p. 54] Empirical equations such as Kozeny-Carman and Hazen equations have been modified recently to account for both relative density and grain size distributions of soils. These equations can be used to develop site-specific k-values.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-8b(1), printed p. 54. The manual prints this subparagraph without a heading; the title is its opening words.

sections.title: A modified version of the Kozeny-Carman equation, as proposed by Chapuis and …
sections.body:
[p. 54] A modified version of the Kozeny-Carman equation, as proposed by Chapuis and Aubertin (2003) requires a complete gradation curve (both sieve and hydrometer), as it accounts for the surface area of the particles. In the absence of hydrometer tests, the estimated k-values could tend higher, as the tail portion of the grain size distribution impacts the estimate. Equation 3-30 (Chapuis 2004) provides a relationship for hydraulic conductivity values based on void ratio (e) and D10 (mm) values, which is considered a modification of the original Hazen (1911) equation. Equation 3-30 is applicable to sand and gravel specimens having an effective diameter D10 between 0.13 and 1.98 mm and a void ratio (e) between 0.4 and 1.5.

k = 2.4622 [D10^2 · e0^3/(1 + e0)]^0.7825 [Eq. 3-30]

where:
k = hydraulic conductivity (cm/s)
D10 = particle size corresponding to 10 percent finer on the cumulative particle size distribution curve (mm)
e0 = in situ void ratio

sections.title: Soil stiffness parameters
sections.body:
[p. 54] Soil stiffness parameters used in analysis depend on mode of loading and can be evaluated using laboratory testing, in situ testing, correlation from other soil parameters, or geophysical testing. Soil stiffness parameters are used for evaluating soil deformation due to static or dynamic loadings. Figure 3-14 illustrates the definitions of various forms of elastic moduli in terms of loading and applied boundary conditions. Based on theory of elasticity, equations 3-32 through 3-35 correlate, K, G, E, M with Poisson’s ratio (υ). Units for G, E, M, and K are expressed in stress/strain format using same unit system, such as English or Metric system. Evaluation of bulk modulus and constrained modulus is complicated when Poisson’s ratio (υ) approaches 0.5 due to the term (1 − 2υ) in the denominator of the equation.

[p. 55] Poisson's ratio, υ = −εh/εv [Eq. 3-31]

Bulk modulus, K = E/(3(1 − 2υ)) [Eq. 3-32]

Shear modulus, G = E/(2(1 + υ)) [Eq. 3-33]

Elastic modulus, E = (9K · G)/(3K + G) [Eq. 3-34]

Constrained modulus, M = (E(1 − υ))/((1 + υ)(1 − 2υ)) [Eq. 3-35]

where:
υ = Poisson’s ratio
εh = horizontal strain, in/in
εv = vertical strain, in/in

sections.title: Poisson’s ratio
sections.body:
[p. 56] Poisson’s ratio. Poisson’s ratio is defined as the ratio of the change in width per unit width of a material, to the change in its length per unit length, as a result of strain. Typical values of Poisson’s ratio (υ) are shown in Table 3-14. For isotropic elastic materials, the range of υ is from 0 to 0.5. A perfectly incompressible (no volume change under applied deformation) isotropic material deformed elastically at small strains would [p. 57] have a Poisson’s ratio of exactly 0.5. Materials that do not deform in the lateral direction (such as cork) under elastic compression have a Poisson’s ratio that approaches zero.

Loose Sand | drained | 0.10 to 0.30

sections.title: Elastic modulus
sections.body: [p. 57] Elastic modulus. Modulus of elasticity is an important soil property for elastic settlement analysis of foundations and for estimation of dynamic soil behavior. In many foundation settlement formulas, the elastic modulus (E) is the stiffness parameter routinely used. The elastic modulus can be defined in different ways along the stress-strain curve as illustrated in Figure 3-16. The elastic modulus definition commonly referenced for shallow foundation design is the secant modulus determined at about 1/2 the deviator stress (Das 2008). When soils show nearly linear behavior in a stress range, the secant modulus definition and tangent definition are nearly the same.

sections.title: The elastic modulus of undrained clay (Eu) is commonly used to estimate the …
sections.body: [p. 57] The elastic modulus of undrained clay (Eu) is commonly used to estimate the immediate settlement of a saturated clay due to foundation loading. The elastic modulus can be determined using in situ tests, triaxial shear strength testing on undisturbed samples, or estimated from correlations with other soil properties. Eu can be correlated with the undrained shear strength by the relationship shown in equation 3-36, with β being correlated to OCR and plasticity. D’Appolonia et al. (1971) published results of ten large-scale field studies that found correlation between Eu, undrained shear strength, soil sensitivity, overconsolidation ratio, and plasticity index.

sections.title: D’Appolonia et al
sections.body:
[p. 57] D’Appolonia et al. also concluded that for highly plastic clays, the laboratory-consolidated, undrained shear tests provided a close approximation of field behavior and unconfined compression. It was also observed that unconsolidated, undrained tests significantly underestimated Eu, and for most clays, consolidated undrained Triaxial tests (both CIU and CKoU) resulted in similar Eu to the measured field conditions. Duncan and Buchagani (1976) advanced the work, compiling results of various studies and published a graph (Figure 3-15) and table relating the undrained elastic modulus of clay to undrained shear strength, soil plasticity, and overconsolidation, as shown in Table 3-15.

sections.title: Elastic modulus from in situ deformation tests
sections.body: [p. 59] Elastic modulus from in situ deformation tests. Flat plate DMT and pressuremeter tests (PMT) are two in situ test “deformation” methods that are commonly used to test the stiffness of the ground in situ. The elastic modulus (E) has been related empirically to the pressuremeter modulus (Eo) by a rheological coefficient (see paragraph 4-10d(4)) and can be estimated by determining the shear modulus (G) using cavity expansion theory. If required, E can also be derived from the DMT modulus (MDMT) using the theory of elasticity. For a Poisson’s ratio of ~ 0.2, theory of elasticity provides E = 0.9M . In view of this approximation, E and M are often used interchangeably.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-9b(2), printed p. 59.

sections.title: Elastic modulus from laboratory triaxial tests
sections.body:
[p. 59] Elastic modulus from laboratory triaxial tests. Consolidated, undrained triaxial testing of clay soils reasonably approximates field conditions. As stiffness of soil depends on the confining pressure, strain level, stress level, and drainage conditions, different definitions of modulus of elasticity (E) can be used, considering the application. Figure 3-16 illustrates a representative stress-strain curve of a soil in triaxial compression mode with different types of modulus of elasticity values (Rix et al. 2018). The type of modulus of elasticity (E) is defined by the loading conditions and specific point on the stress-strain curve, such as (1) initial modulus (Emax), (2) secant modulus, Esec = q/εa, (3) tangent modulus, Etan = Δq/εa, and (4) unload-reload modulus, Eur. For foundation design, it is typical to use the secant modulus at 1/2 of the deviator stress.

sections.body:
[p. 60] The elastic modulus for sand and gravel is best determined by in situ testing, either directly or through correlation with strength measurements. Table 3-16 summarizes the general range of E that can be expected (Das 2017), and equations 3-37, 7-16, and 7-17 provide formulas correlating E with SPT and CPT measurements. The horizontal stress-strain can be directly measured using the flat plate DMT or E can be estimated from SPT and CPT measurements. DMT testing to estimate elastic modulus and constrained modulus is presented in paragraph 3-9c(2).

sections.title: Correlations with standard penetration test data
sections.body:
[p. 61] Correlations with standard penetration test data. Correlation of E with SPT blowcount data is inherently approximate and much scatter is observed in the literature. It is generally better to use CPT or DMT measurements to estimate E, due the higher degree of reliability and repeatability. Codutu (2016) identifies equation 3-37 to estimate E from SPT data, as it is noted to be generally conservative. In general, an OCR equal to 1 is assumed unless there is compelling evidence otherwise.

E = β0 √OCR + β1 N60 [Eq. 3-37]

where:
E = elastic modulus (psf)
βo and β1 = factors related to soil classification, see Table 3-17
N60 = corrected SPT N-value for field procedures, per equation 4-4 (blows/ft)
OCR = overconsolidation ratio

sections.title: Unsaturated soils
sections.body: [p. 61] Unsaturated soils. For soils, the elastic modulus varies in relation to degree of saturation. The higher the degree of saturation, the lower the elastic modulus. This is especially true for clay, and much less significant for sand. Lu and Kaya (2013) proposed a power-law relationship to relate the elastic modulus E to the degree of saturation. The elastic modulus is a maximum when the soil is dry and minimum when the specimen is wet. For some clays evaluated by Lu and Kaya, the ratio of Emin to Emax was as low as about 0.1 but was generally negligible for sand with intermediate levels of reduction for silts. For most static foundation designs on clay, it is conservative to use E from saturated undrained testing.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-9b(5), printed p. 61.

sections.title: Constrained modulus
sections.body: [p. 61] Constrained modulus. The constrained modulus (M) is used in the one-dimensional (1-D) analysis of consolidation settlement and is simply the ratio of axial stress to axial strain in confined compression. The constrained modulus (M) can be determined from laboratory oedometer test data (see paragraph 7-7) as the inverse of the coefficient of volume compressibility (mv) or correlated with in situ test data. For an ideal elastic soil, M is related to the elastic modulus by equation 3-35. Codutu (2016) indicates that the constrained modulus is commonly used for settlement analysis (as opposed to the e-log-p method) when the soil is overconsolidated and behaves in a linear way, and when strain vs load is plotted on a linear scale.

sections.title: Constrained modulus from cone penetration test
sections.body:
[p. 61] Constrained modulus from cone penetration test. Existing correlations between constrained modulus and cone resistance typically have the form shown in equation 3-38.

[p. 62] M = αM(qt − σv0) [Eq. 3-38]

where:
M = constrained modulus (tsf)
αM = constrained modulus cone factor (dimensionless), see Note
qt = corrected tip resistance (tsf), see Table 4-7
σv0 = total vertical stress (tsf)

Note. Mayne (2006) showed that αM varies with soil type and net cone resistance with values of 1 to 10, where the low values apply to soft clays. Robertson and Cabal (2022) related the coefficient αM to the normalized cone resistance (Qt) and the soil behavior index (Ic) as shown in equations 3-39a, 3-39b, and 3-40.

sections.title: Constrained modulus from dilatometer
sections.body:
[p. 62] Constrained modulus from dilatometer. The DMT constrained modulus (M or MDMT) is obtained at the pre-insertion in situ vertical effective stress (σ′vo). MDMT is the vertical drained confined tangent modulus. MDMT is calculated by applying a correction factor to the DMT modulus (ED). MDMT should be used in the same way as the constrained modulus determined from laboratory oedometer testing, reference paragraph 7-7. For sand or clay, MDMT can be calculated per equation 3-41 using the correction factor RM. The equations defining RM = f(ID, KD) were established by Marchetti (1980).

Constrained Modulus, MDMT = RM · ED [Eq. 3-41]

RM = 0.14 + 2.36 log KD   for ID ≤ 0.6 [Eq. 3-41a]

RM = RM,0 + (2.5 − RM,0) log KD   for 0.6 < ID < 3, with RM,0 = 0.14 + 0.15(ID − 0.6) [Eq. 3-41b]

RM = 0.5 + 2.0 log KD   for ID > 3 [Eq. 3-41c]

[p. 63] RM = 0.32 + 2.18 log KD   for KD > 10 [Eq. 3-41d]

where:
MDMT = constrained modulus from DMT (bar); note that 1 bar ≈ 1.044 tsf
RM = correction factor for converting ED to MDMT; if RM is calculated to be less than 0.85, set RM = 0.85
ED = DMT modulus, see equation 4-15
KD = horizontal stress index, see equation 4-14
ID = material index, see equation 4-13

Note. The correction factor (RM) is a function of the intermediate DMT parameters (KD and ID). KD typically varies in the range of 2 to 20, with corresponding values of RM in the range of 1 to 3 (Marchetti et al. 2001). Typically, MDMT varies in the range of 4 to 4,000 bar (~ 4.18 tsf to 4,177 tsf).

sections.title: Bulk and shear modulus
sections.body: [p. 63] Bulk and shear modulus. Bulk modulus (K) and shear modulus (G) are not used in typical hand-calculation formulations for routine foundation design. For some numerical analyses, the constitutive models require the use of K and G as model inputs.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-9d, printed p. 63.

sections.title: Bulk modulus
sections.body: [p. 63] Bulk modulus. The bulk modulus (K) is not used directly in most routine calculations for foundation design. The bulk modulus is more commonly used in non-linear elastic stress models such as Duncan and Chang (1970) to model stress-dependent stiffness changes, which is further described in Duncan (1980).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 3 (Soil Properties), paragraph 3-9d(1), printed p. 63.

sections.title: Shear strain modulus
sections.body:
[p. 63] Shear strain modulus. The shear strain modulus is a non-linear function, which is defined by the initial or small-strain modulus and relationships to describe the shear modulus reduction at larger strains. For static foundation problems, shear strain is typically about 1/2 percent. The initial, or small, strain shear modulus (Gmax) is commonly determined using in situ shear wave velocity measurements. Geophysical tests such as crosshole seismic tests and suspension logging or surface geophysical methods (from free field) or downhole seismic tests (from free field) measure shear wave velocity (Vs), of soils. Shear wave velocity data can be used to calculate Gmax of soil using equation 3-42. Typical values for small strain shear modulus are provided in Table 3-18.

Gmax = ρ · Vs^2 [Eq. 3-42]

where:
Gmax = initial or small strain shear modulus (psf)
ρ = density [total unit weight of soil, γt (pcf) / g (acceleration due to gravity, ft/sec^2)]
Vs = shear wave velocity (ft/sec)

sections.title: Initial or small-strain shear modulus
sections.body:
[p. 64] Initial or small-strain shear modulus. Small-strain shear modulus (G) depends on in situ confining pressure and packing conditions of soil particles. A few common relationships to estimate the initial or maximum shear modulus are provided in equations 3-43 through 3-46. These relations use SPT N-values or relative density for coarse-grained soils and void ratio and stress history for fine-grained soils.

Gmax = 21.7 K2max · Pa (σ′m/Pa)^(1/2) [Eq. 3-43]

K2max = 20[(N1)60cs]^0.33   (Seed et al. 1984) [Eq. 3-44]

K2max = 0.6DR + 15   (Byrne et al. 1987) [Eq. 3-45]

K2max = 625 OCR^k/(0.3 + 0.7 e^2)   (Hardin 1978) [Eq. 3-46]

where:
K2max = modulus coefficient for estimating Gmax
Pa = atmospheric pressure (at sea level Pa ≈ 2,116 psf or 101.3 kPa)
σ′m = mean normal effective stress (same unit as Pa)
(N1)60cs = normalized SPT N-Value using Youd et al. (2001) or Boulanger and Idriss (2015) or Cetin et al. (2018) methods, as used in analysis
DR = relative density (percent)
OCR = overconsolidation ratio (dimensionless)
k = function of PI and OCR
e = initial void ratio (dimensionless)

sections.title: G/Gmax relationships
sections.body: [p. 64] G/Gmax relationships. The shear modulus for the shallow foundation needs to be reduced from the Gmax level, considering the loading and strain condition. A full shear modulus curve can be estimated using the G/Gmax relationships by Darendeli (2001) for clay and sand and Menq (2003) relationship for gravel or other appropriate soil-type-specific relationships based on local experience or laboratory testing. A strength correction considering the soil strength should be performed according to Stewart et al. (2014). The full curves are commonly used in dynamic numerical analysis where the shear strain and modulus values change during the course of dynamic loading.

sections.title: Shear modulus for shallow foundations
sections.body:
[p. 65] Shear modulus for shallow foundations. Shear modulus (G) values vary with strain. The allowable strain depends on structure type and design objectives. Figure 3-17 conceptually shows shear modulus (G) versus shear strain relationship and the allowable stress range for different types of structures, including shallow foundations. For most static shallow foundation applications, G is about 0.1 to 0.05 of Gmax (Das 1997), although sensitive buildings or machines may require smaller strain levels.

sections.title: Shear wave velocity from standard and cone penetration tests
sections.body: [p. 65] Shear wave velocity from standard and cone penetration tests. Seismic CPT or other surface or borehole geophysical methods can measure shear wave velocity, which can then be used to calculate Gmax. In the absence of field measurement of shear wave velocity (Vs) from seismic CPTs or other geophysical methods, empirical relationships can be used. Wair et al. (2012) provides empirical relationships for Vs estimation from SPT and CPT data. Some of these relationships were developed using SPT energy ratio of 67 percent or 78 percent, commonly used in Japan. A conversion factor of 1.12 or 1.3 between the U.S. SPT N-value and the Japanese N-value should be used [SPT N(U.S.) = 1.12 or 1.3 SPT N (Japan)] while converting relationships that have been developed using Japanese SPT N-values. Uncertainty in Vs to SPT or CPT is high and site-specific relationships are preferred.
